GitPizza · performance under load · 19 November 2026

GitPizza Load Test

Two guest journeys measured against a year of a busy store: 400,059 orders and about ten million rows. Each step ran six times; figures are medians of the five warm runs, before and after the fixes this test led to, counting only the guest's own requests (the simulator's background clock is left out).

259 89 msDatabase time to add a configured pizza to the cart (465 → 317 queries)

Every step, before and after

Browser time runs from the click until the last request it set off has answered (with the median's min–max underneath). Server time is the sum of the guest's request spans, database time the sum of their JDBC spans. Highlighted rows are the steps the fixes target. The others did not change: their Δ is run-to-run spread on this machine — "place order and pay" and "open tracking" land on one of two plateaus set by the simulator's tick (F8), and the 2-second live poller can fall inside a short step's window. Server and database time are the steadier measure there.

Findings

F1
Fixed · locking

Housekeeping held a 10-minute transaction and blocked every checkout

Every 15 minutes the simulator's tick runs housekeeping (SIM-08): it removes simulated orders and simulation events older than 24 hours. It loaded all of them and deleted them in one transaction. With a backlog of 800,089 events — what housekeeping that was off or failing leaves behind — that transaction ran from 16:03:00 until the runtime aborted it at 16:13:02. It held the store-settings row it had locked to number a new order, so every guest's Execute Order --force waited on that lock and the step timed out; the watchdog restarted the clock every minute, and the abort rolled back the "last run" time too, so the next tick started the same delete again. In this state the shop takes no orders at all.

Fix: Simulation.SIM_Housekeeping deletes oldest-first in batches of 1,000 events and 50 orders per tick, and marks the run done only when a batch comes back short; an index on SimulationEvent.OccurredAt finds the batch. Measured on the same backlog: housekeeping 28 ms per tick (max 76), the whole tick 75 ms (max 171), and all twelve steps ran during the drain — "place order and pay" in 5,842 ms, as without a backlog.

F2
Fixed · index

The home KPIs scanned every order ever placed

Shop.SUB_Home_Refresh counts the orders completed today: [(OrderStatus = DELIVERED or PICKED_UP) and CompletedAt >= today]. Without an index on CompletedAt Postgres read all 400,059 orders on every home page: 63.5 ms per call. Fix: index on Order.CompletedAt: 5.4 ms, reading only today's rows. Database time of the home step 91 → 34 ms.

F3
Fixed · index

The traffic generator and housekeeping scanned every order too

The traffic generator counts open simulated orders before it spawns one ([Source = SIMULATOR and IsOpen], 54 ms) and housekeeping looks for finished simulated orders past their retention (… and StatusChangedAt < cutoff, 48 ms). Both were sequential scans, because guest orders — the whole history — match neither. Fix: one index on Order(Source, IsOpen, StatusChangedAt) serves both; the housekeeping query now reads the index only (0.07 ms in EXPLAIN ANALYZE). These run in the background, so no guest step shows them, but they ran every few seconds against the full table.

F4
Fixed · query

The menu ran a data source for every product card

Each card's code block listed the toppings through a nested list fed by Shop.DS_Product_Recipe: twelve microflow calls and their association reads per menu render, and again whenever the menu refreshed after an add. Fix: the toppings line is stored on the product (CodeToppings) by Shop.SUB_Product_Recalculate, like the card's other derived values, and recalculated at every start. Menu: 199 → 75 queries, browser 418 → 224 ms.

F5
Fixed · query

Configuring a pizza cost two queries per option and per ingredient

Shop.DS_Config_Choices read each option's ingredient twice to decide stock (once in Catalog.SUB_Option_AvailableFor), and Shop.SUB_Line_Recalculate read each recipe item's ingredient and its allergens one by one. Fix: one query for the options whose ingredient is out of stock, one for the recipe's ingredients (found in memory per item) and, without removed toppings, one for their allergens; a new Catalog.SUB_Option_Selectable decides availability without database access. Queries: configurator 305 → 195, choose extra 299 → 189, add to cart 465 → 317 (database 259 → 89 ms). The configurator's browser time did not improve: its server work fell (594 → 358 ms), but the median after-run caught one 2-second live-poll request inside its window (see "How it was measured").

F6
Open · recommendation

Adding to the cart still recalculates every line several times

An add runs SUB_Line_Recalculate for the new line in SUB_Config_Commit and twice in SUB_Cart_AddLine, then once per cart line in SUB_Cart_Recalculate, so its cost grows with the cart (up to 30 items). The configurator also calls DS_Config_Choices once per tile group (seven times), each re-checking cart ownership and re-reading product and size: still 195 queries. Recommended: recalculate only the changed line and refresh the cart totals from stored line values; build all tile groups in one data source.

F7
Open · recommendation

The home KPIs still load the day's orders to count them

With the index the query is fast, but SUB_Home_Refresh still retrieves every order completed today (about 1,100 a day at this volume) to count them and average their pipeline time in a loop. A view entity (OQL COUNT/AVG, Mendix 10.18+) lets the database return the two numbers — the project's own convention for aggregates.

F8
By design

"Place order and pay" takes 3.8 or 5.8 seconds

The simulated gateway takes 3 seconds (lite-configuration: paymentProcessing), and the payment sheet advances when the simulator's next tick and the next 2-second poll have both happened, so the step lands on one of two plateaus: before 3,812–5,831 ms, after 3,833–5,841 ms. Its server and database work did not change (102 → 103 ms). "Open tracking" right after it shows the same two-plateau spread. Neither is a regression.

OK
No change needed

Finding a past order stays fast at 400,000 orders

The lookup by order number and email (13 ms database) and opening an old order's tracking link (23 ms) use the unique indexes on OrderNumber and TrackingToken that were there from the start; their times are the same as on the 59-order demo data.

How it was measured

  • Seed: docs/perf/tools/seed.sql (direct SQL with the runtime's id formula, dates relative to now); backup taken first and restored afterwards.
  • Postgres 16 with pg_stat_statements and auto_explain (20 ms) for the runs, then reset; the app on the local runtime with OpenTelemetry to an OTLP collector.
  • tests/perf/journeys.js: "Guest orders a pizza" (9 steps) and "Guest finds a past order" (3 steps on seeded order MX-200000), six runs each, run 0 is warm-up. A step ends when no request has started for 0.6 s.
  • "Before" is the committed model on the seed, "after" the fixed model on the same seed, both from a fresh start. docs/perf/tools/analyse.py keeps only traces rooted in a guest request on the app port; mxcli report performance's own JSON is kept next to it (*-raw.json).
  • F1 was observed on the first run of the committed model with a year of simulation events; the "after" drain ran the journeys while the same backlog was being removed.

Limits

  • One machine, one guest at a time: no concurrency or contention beyond the simulator.
  • The page's 2-second live poller can land inside a step window and add up to ~200 ms of browser time; compare server and database time for small steps.
  • The seed is uniform: every order is a finished guest order, ~1,100 a day. Real traffic has peaks and more open orders.
  • Payment is simulated (3 s by design), so "place order and pay" says little about real gateway latency.
